patient.chief_complaint: Woke up with slurred speech and right-sided clumsiness
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Curtis Darnell is a 67-year-old right-handed African American man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, and a prior transient ischemic attack who was brought to the emergency department by his wife after she noticed something was wrong when he woke up this morning. His wife reports that he went to bed at approximately 22:30 last night and was entirely at his baseline, having watched the evening news and conversed normally before falling asleep. She awoke at 06:15 this morning and found him already sitting on the edge of the bed. He told her he felt 'off' and she immediately noticed his speech was slurred. When he tried to stand, he stumbled slightly to the right side and had difficulty buttoning his shirt with his right hand. She drove him to the emergency department, arriving at 07:40. The patient himself reports that he woke up around 06:00 and noticed his right hand felt 'clumsy' and his mouth felt 'thick.' He denies any headache, visual changes, nausea, or vomiting. He did not experience any chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath. There was no witnessed seizure activity. He denies any recent fever, neck stiffness, or trauma. He admits he has not been taking his blood pressure medications consistently over the past week because he ran out and had not yet refilled the prescriptions. He also acknowledges continued smoking despite medical advice. His wife notes that he has been snoring more heavily than usual over the past several months and has not been using his CPAP device for over a year. She recalls his prior TIA episode two years ago presented similarly with transient right hand clumsiness that resolved within an hour, but this time the symptoms have persisted. Last known well time is established as 22:30 the prior evening, approximately 9 hours before ED arrival, placing him outside the standard IV tPA window.

output.query: wake-up stroke thrombolysis tissue clock DWI-FLAIR mismatch management guidelines

results.title: MRI-Guided Thrombolysis for Stroke with Unknown Time of Onset (WAKE-UP Trial)
results.authors: Thomalla G, Simonsen CZ, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase guided by DWI-FLAIR mismatch (DWI positive, FLAIR negative) resulted in better functional outcomes compared to placebo in wake-up stroke patients. DWI-FLAIR mismatch suggests stroke onset within approximately 4.5 hours.

results.title: Extending the Time for Thrombolysis in Emergency Neurological Deficits (EXTEND Trial)
results.authors: Ma H, Campbell BCV, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase 4.5-9 hours after onset (or wake-up stroke) improved outcomes when guided by perfusion imaging showing salvageable penumbra.

results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guideline Update: Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke
results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: For wake-up strokes, IV alteplase may be considered if DWI-FLAIR mismatch is present, suggesting stroke occurred within 4.5 hours. If FLAIR is already positive, patient is likely outside the safe thrombolysis window.

output.summary: In wake-up stroke, the DWI-FLAIR mismatch concept serves as a tissue clock to identify patients who may benefit from IV thrombolysis despite unknown onset time. A DWI-positive/FLAIR-negative pattern suggests onset within approximately 4.5 hours and may support thrombolysis eligibility (WAKE-UP trial, NEJM 2018). When FLAIR is already positive, the infarct is likely older than 4.5 hours, and IV thrombolysis is generally not recommended. CT perfusion-guided approaches (EXTEND trial, NEJM 2019) offer an alternative pathway for late-window patients with salvageable penumbra. For patients with proximal vascular occlusion, thrombectomy remains an option up to 24 hours based on perfusion imaging criteria (DAWN, DEFUSE-3).

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW) and apply NIHSS to determine acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes if IV thrombolysis is indicated
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg prior to IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
Initiate continuous telemetry and obtain prolonged cardiac monitoring to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Begin secondary prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) and high-intensity statin per mechanism
Recognize the wake-up presentation: apply DWI-FLAIR mismatch (WAKE-UP) or perfusion mismatch (EXTEND) criteria for late-window thrombolysis decision
Pursue prolonged cardiac monitoring despite sinus rhythm on initial ECG, given left atrial enlargement
Transition from antiplatelet to oral anticoagulation once paroxysmal AF is documented (timing per infarct size and hemorrhage risk)
Consult vascular surgery for symptomatic 60-69% left ICA stenosis with high-risk plaque features (consider carotid endarterectomy or stenting)
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other guideline-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening penumbral perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation in the acute phase of a large infarct without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not administer IV tPA in this wake-up stroke without first confirming DWI-FLAIR mismatch — FLAIR positivity places the infarct outside the safe thrombolysis window
Do not stop investigation at 'atherosclerotic stroke' on the basis of an initial sinus ECG — left atrial enlargement mandates prolonged monitoring
Avoid full-dose iodinated contrast in CKD without renal protection or use of MRA alternative

key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
proximal vascular occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
DWI-FLAIR mismatch is the tissue clock for unknown-onset (wake-up) strokes; FLAIR positivity in this case indicates onset >4.5h before imaging
Symptomatic 60-69% ICA stenosis with irregular hypoechoic plaque is a high-risk lesion and an independent therapeutic target (surgical or endovascular revascularization)

Concurrent paroxysmal AF and symptomatic carotid stenosis create a mixed mechanism: anticoagulation addresses cardioembolic risk while carotid revascularization addresses the artery-to-artery component
CKD stage 3a mandates contrast caution; MR angiography or duplex ultrasound are preferred alternatives when feasible
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
